verdicts.quote: readBytes() method at line 83 reads an unsigned 32-bit integer at line 86: final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt()). This value is then used directly to allocate a byte array at line 88: final byte[] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength]. No bounds checking is performed on contentLength before allocation.
verdicts.why: F04 is exactly the mechanism: a length field (contentLength) taken from the untrusted AMQP frame determines the size of the allocation, and the byte[] is created immediately from that value with no check that the declared payload actually exists or is available. The exploit it describes (contentLength near Integer.MAX_VALUE causing immediate OutOfMemoryError before any message data is read) is the attacker-controlled-length-drives-premature-allocation defect.

verdicts.quote: readTable() method at line 139 recursively calls readFieldValue() at line 150. readFieldValue() at line 158 switches on type byte and calls readTable() again at line 181 (case 'F') and readArray() at line 184 (case 'A'). readArray() at line 237 recursively calls readFieldValue() at line 245. No depth limit is enforced on recursion.
verdicts.why: F02 is exactly the mechanism: it traces the mutual-recursion cycle among the decoding routines (readTable -> readFieldValue -> readTable/readArray -> readFieldValue), states that no depth counter bounds the cycle, and identifies the exploit as nesting depth in the attacker-supplied frame driving recursion until StackOverflowError.
